source.authors: Moffitt TB, Atcherson S, Padberg J
source.title: Auditory brainstem responses in the nine-banded armadillo (Dasypus novemcinctus)

method: auditory brainstem response (ABR) to tone bursts (2 ms rise-plateau-fall, 6 ms total) at 13 frequencies from 0.5 to 48 kHz, delivered by a hollow tube with a foam tip in the ear canal; threshold is the lowest level meeting a peak I amplitude criterion of twice the maximum background response; an electrophysiological threshold in dB peSPL, not a behavioural audiogram
conditions: eight wild-caught adult armadillos (3 female, 5 male, 3.8 to 6 kg in the Methods (Table 1 lists 3.4 to 5.3 kg); capture site not stated) housed at 22 C; anaesthetised with isoflurane 1.75 to 2.5 % by nose mask; stimulation rate 27.7/s, 1,000 to 1,200 sweeps averaged; calibration against a 94 dB SPL 1 kHz tone with a piston phone; number tested varies by frequency (Table 2); ear not stated in the Methods (Figure 1 shows the right ear, Figure 3 the left); recording-room conditions not stated
quote: Across all cases, the lowest thresholds were observed for frequencies from 8 to 12 kHz.
note: Value is the band of lowest ABR thresholds (best sensitivity), not the hearing range. ABR thresholds usually sit above behavioural thresholds. Printed name Dasypus novemcinctus (the paper calls it 'the only extant North American member of superclade Xenarthra'; wild-caught, capture site not stated; IACUC University of Central Arkansas). The Mammal Diversity Database now restricts D. novemcinctus Linnaeus, 1758 to South America (taxon/1000424) and places the armadillos of the southern USA, Arkansas included, in Dasypus mexicanus Peters, 1865, split from D. novemcinctus by Barthe et al. 2024, Systematic Biology 74(2): 177-197 (taxon/1006877).

value: only 2 of 5 animals responded at 48 kHz, the highest frequency tested; mean threshold 39.1 dB peSPL (SD 12.01), maximum stimulus level presented 52.8 dB peSPL
method: auditory brainstem response (ABR) to tone bursts (2 ms rise-plateau-fall, 6 ms total) at 13 frequencies from 0.5 to 48 kHz, delivered by a hollow tube with a foam tip in the ear canal; threshold is the lowest level meeting a peak I amplitude criterion of twice the maximum background response; an electrophysiological threshold in dB peSPL, not a behavioural audiogram

note: Row reads: 48 kHz; 2 of 5 animals responsive; minimum threshold 30.3 dB peSPL; mean 39.1; SD 12.01; maximum stimulus level 52.8 dB peSPL. The top of the stimulus set is 48 kHz and the maximum level at that frequency was low, so the non-responders do not show deafness above 48 kHz or at higher levels. source.authors: Keary N, Ruploh T, Voss J, Thalau P, Wiltschko R, Wiltschko W, Bischof H-J
source.title: Oscillating magnetic field disrupts magnetic orientation in Zebra finches, Taeniopygia guttata

value: significantly oriented in the field shifted horizontally by 90 degrees: mean score 0.74 (+/- 0.098 SD), n = 7
method: behavioural: a cubic non-magnetic plastic box (80 x 80 x 80 cm) with a food tray behind a screen in each of its four corners; magnetically trained birds found food at the two trays at both ends of the magnetic north-south axis (an axial task, chance 0.5), the east-west trays covered with transparent mesh; visually trained birds found food in one direction marked by coloured landmarks, the setup rotated before each trial (chance 0.25); test condition 1 = horizontal field component shifted clockwise by 90 degrees with a 2 m Helmholtz coil; condition 2 = condition 1 plus a 1.156 MHz oscillating field (local Larmor frequency, 0.47 uT, about 1 % of the local field) from a coil antenna around the arena, applied during tests only; score = number of correct choices / all choices, first tray inspected counted
conditions: local field 43 uT, inclination 67 degrees; 10 birds (5 male, 5 female) in the magnetic experiment, 7 (4 male, 3 female) of them reached the learning criterion and are the n = 7 analysed; each bird tested ten times in each of two conditions; birds from the institute breeding colony; the arena was homogeneously illuminated (whether tests ran in light or dark is not stated); a control group trained to visual landmarks was tested under the same two magnetic conditions
quote: Statistical analysis revealed that with a mean score of 0.74 (± 0.098 SD) the birds were significantly oriented in the 90° horizontally shifted field (n = 7, t = 6.58, p = 0.0006) (fig. 2).
note: Shows a magnetic compass in a short-distance food-search task (captive, trained). It gives no sensitivity threshold. Taeniopygia guttata (Vieillot, 1817) is the species the paper prints and the IOC World Bird Names list (worldbirdnames.com) accepts, with the Australian form castanotis as a subspecies; some checklists treat castanotis as a separate species. Licence: the Springer page states Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY 2.0), BioMed Central.

source.authors: Keary N, Ruploh T, Voss J, Thalau P, Wiltschko R, Wiltschko W, Bischof H-J
source.title: Oscillating magnetic field disrupts magnetic orientation in Zebra finches, Taeniopygia guttata

value: group orientation lost with the 1.156 MHz oscillating field added: mean score 0.49 (+/- 0.17 SD), n = 7, not different from random (reference 0.5); six of seven birds' scores fell, one bird (b6) scored 0.8 in both conditions
method: behavioural: a cubic non-magnetic plastic box (80 x 80 x 80 cm) with a food tray behind a screen in each of its four corners; magnetically trained birds found food at the two trays at both ends of the magnetic north-south axis (an axial task, chance 0.5), the east-west trays covered with transparent mesh; visually trained birds found food in one direction marked by coloured landmarks, the setup rotated before each trial (chance 0.25); test condition 1 = horizontal field component shifted clockwise by 90 degrees with a 2 m Helmholtz coil; condition 2 = condition 1 plus a 1.156 MHz oscillating field (local Larmor frequency, 0.47 uT, about 1 % of the local field) from a coil antenna around the arena, applied during tests only; score = number of correct choices / all choices, first tray inspected counted
conditions: local field 43 uT, inclination 67 degrees; 10 birds (5 male, 5 female) in the magnetic experiment, 7 (4 male, 3 female) of them reached the learning criterion and are the n = 7 analysed; each bird tested ten times in each of two conditions; birds from the institute breeding colony; the arena was homogeneously illuminated (whether tests ran in light or dark is not stated); a control group trained to visual landmarks was tested under the same two magnetic conditions
quote: The t-test over all birds (n = 7) revealed that the mean score of 0.49 (± 0.17 SD) with the oscillating field added did not differ from random … (fig. 2A).
note: The cut removes the test statistics (reference value 0.5, t = -0.23, p = 0.83). A radio-frequency disruption of this kind is the paper's argument for a radical-pair mechanism over magnetite, which is the authors' inference, not shown directly. Taeniopygia guttata (Vieillot, 1817) is the species the paper prints and the IOC World Bird Names list (worldbirdnames.com) accepts, with the Australian form castanotis as a subspecies; some checklists treat castanotis as a separate species. Licence: the Springer page states Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY 2.0), BioMed Central. Results: 'With scores of 0.8, one bird, however, was oriented in both test conditions.' Individual scores in Table 1; the authors think chance more likely for this bird (Discussion). Shifted field versus shifted field plus oscillating field: Wilcoxon Z = 2.2, p = 0.028, n = 7.

eye: not isolated to an organ; the paper infers a radical-pair receptor (retina proposed), not tested for location here

source.authors: Keary N, Ruploh T, Voss J, Thalau P, Wiltschko R, Wiltschko W, Bischof H-J
source.title: Oscillating magnetic field disrupts magnetic orientation in Zebra finches, Taeniopygia guttata

value: visually trained control birds showed no difference in orientation performance between the two magnetic conditions (shifted field, and shifted field plus oscillating field)
method: behavioural: a cubic non-magnetic plastic box (80 x 80 x 80 cm) with a food tray behind a screen in each of its four corners; magnetically trained birds found food at the two trays at both ends of the magnetic north-south axis (an axial task, chance 0.5), the east-west trays covered with transparent mesh; visually trained birds found food in one direction marked by coloured landmarks, the setup rotated before each trial (chance 0.25); test condition 1 = horizontal field component shifted clockwise by 90 degrees with a 2 m Helmholtz coil; condition 2 = condition 1 plus a 1.156 MHz oscillating field (local Larmor frequency, 0.47 uT, about 1 % of the local field) from a coil antenna around the arena, applied during tests only; score = number of correct choices / all choices, first tray inspected counted
conditions: local field 43 uT, inclination 67 degrees; 10 birds (5 male, 5 female) in the magnetic experiment, 7 (4 male, 3 female) of them reached the learning criterion and are the n = 7 analysed; each bird tested ten times in each of two conditions; birds from the institute breeding colony; the arena was homogeneously illuminated (whether tests ran in light or dark is not stated); a control group trained to visual landmarks was tested under the same two magnetic conditions; controls were scored against a chance reference of 0.25 in the paper's t test
quote: Birds that were trained to visually guided orientation showed no difference of orientation performance in the two magnetic conditions.
note: Control: the oscillating field did not impair visually guided orientation (mean scores 0.9 +/- 0.14 SD without and 0.87 +/- 0.14 SD with the oscillating field, n = 7), so the loss of orientation in magnetically trained birds is not a general disturbance. Taeniopygia guttata (Vieillot, 1817) is the species the paper prints and the IOC World Bird Names list (worldbirdnames.com) accepts, with the Australian form castanotis as a subspecies; some checklists treat castanotis as a separate species. source.authors: Ruscher B, Sills JM, Richter BP, Reichmuth C
source.title: In-air hearing in Hawaiian monk seals: implications for understanding the auditory biology of Monachinae seals

method: behavioural audiogram: go/no-go psychophysics with an adaptive staircase, threshold at 50 % correct detection; 500 ms frequency-modulated upsweeps (10 % bandwidth); 11 frequencies from 0.1 to 25.6 kHz in octave steps plus 18.1 and 33.2 kHz; functional hearing range defined as the frequencies audible at 60 dB re 20 uPa
conditions: one adult male (KE18, 17 years old, about 200 kg) tested in a hemi-anechoic sound-attenuating chamber at Long Marine Laboratory, UC Santa Cruz, one session a day five days a week over 12 months from April 2019; 40 to 60 trials per session; a single animal; the paper gives no maximum SPL for the full audiogram (90 dB re 20 uPa did not need to be exceeded for the masked tests at 0.8 and 3.2 kHz)
quote: The behavioral audiogram indicates a functional hearing range from 0.1 to 33 kHz and poor sensitivity, with detection thresholds above 40 dB re 20 µPa.
note: Functional range at the 60 dB criterion for one seal. The edges are the lowest (0.1 kHz) and highest (33.2 kHz) frequencies tested, so the audible limits may lie beyond the stimulus set; the authors call 33.2 kHz 'the highest frequency to which KE18 exhibited reliable responses' and describe the range as constrained at both ends compared with Phocinae tested the same way. Printed and accepted name Neomonachus schauinslandi (Matschie, 1906), listed as a species on the Mammal Diversity Database (mammaldiversity.org/taxon/1005921); moved from Monachus per Scheel et al. 2014 (NOAA Fisheries taxonomy note). Licence: the Springer page states Creative Commons Attribution 4.0.

value: best sensitivity: lowest threshold 40 dB re 20 uPa at 0.8 and 3.2 kHz
method: behavioural audiogram: go/no-go psychophysics with an adaptive staircase, threshold at 50 % correct detection; 500 ms frequency-modulated upsweeps (10 % bandwidth); 11 frequencies from 0.1 to 25.6 kHz in octave steps plus 18.1 and 33.2 kHz; functional hearing range defined as the frequencies audible at 60 dB re 20 uPa
conditions: one adult male (KE18, 17 years old, about 200 kg) tested in a hemi-anechoic sound-attenuating chamber at Long Marine Laboratory, UC Santa Cruz, one session a day five days a week over 12 months from April 2019; 40 to 60 trials per session; a single animal; the paper gives no maximum SPL for the full audiogram (90 dB re 20 uPa did not need to be exceeded for the masked tests at 0.8 and 3.2 kHz)
quote: The lowest threshold of 40 dB re 20 μPa was measured at 0.8 and 3.2 kHz, indicating relatively poor overall sensitivity to airborne sounds.
note: The authors read this as poor in-air hearing compared with Phocinae seals tested under the same conditions (the monk seal's best threshold about 50 dB higher, that is poorer, Discussion). One individual. Printed and accepted name Neomonachus schauinslandi (Matschie, 1906), listed as a species on the Mammal Diversity Database (mammaldiversity.org/taxon/1005921); moved from Monachus per Scheel et al. 2014 (NOAA Fisheries taxonomy note).
